questions.q: Why does an organization running many incidents a month need a standardized, org-wide postmortem template instead of each team using its own format?
options: A standard template is required so that executives, not engineers, can write postmortems
Templates are only needed for incidents rated SEV1; smaller incidents don't need any documentation
Without a shared structure, postmortems can't be compared across teams, which makes it nearly impossible to spot repeated causes or let anyone outside the writing team learn from it
It removes the need for a Scribe, since the template itself generates the timeline automatically
questions.explain: A shared format is what makes it possible to compare incidents across teams and spot patterns — this is also the precondition for a review board's cross-postmortem work.

questions.q: Why does a well-designed postmortem template treat "root cause" as plural-friendly rather than forcing a single cause?
options: Legal requirements mandate exactly one named cause per incident report
Most real incidents have several contributing factors, and forcing a single root cause pressures people to oversimplify
It isn't plural-friendly — every mature template requires exactly one root cause
Multiple causes are listed only to spread blame across more teams
questions.explain: A template that forces a single "root" cause pressures people to oversimplify what's usually a combination of contributing factors.

questions.q: What does an action item need, according to this lesson, to actually count as an action item rather than a wish?
options: A named owner and a due date
Nothing more than a general description of the problem
Approval from the postmortem review board before it can even be written down
A severity rating matching the incident's own severity
questions.explain: An action item with neither a named owner nor a due date isn't actually an action item — it's a wish that has no mechanism for getting done.

questions.q: What specific question does a postmortem review board ask that a single team's own retro does not?
options: "Which engineer caused this incident?"
"Should this incident be hidden from the rest of the company?"
"How do we close this incident channel fastest?"
"What's changing across many postmortems that no single team would notice on its own?" — looking for repeated root causes, overdue action items, or a rising severity trend
questions.explain: A single-team retro asks what that team should change. A review board looks across many postmortems for systemic patterns, like the same root cause recurring on unrelated teams.

questions.q: Why is blameless language described as a practical requirement rather than just a tone preference?
options: Blameless postmortems are required to avoid any mention of what went wrong at all
If writing an honest timeline risks individual blame, people write vaguer timelines and omit details, which makes the record less accurate and less useful to the review board
It's purely a legal formality with no effect on what people actually write
Blameless language means no action items are ever assigned to a specific person
questions.explain: Blameless framing focuses on the system and the decision inputs available at the time, which is what keeps the Scribe's timeline and the "what went poorly" section honest enough to be useful.
